body: Gotham Capital (1985): ~50% annualised over its first decade, per Greenblatt's own book You Can Be a Stock Market Genius (1997) - self-reported, not audited (confidence: single-source); outside capital returned in 1994-95. Structural edge (early): small fund size allowed meaningful positions in spin-offs, restructurings, rights offerings, merger securities and LEAPS where institutions are forced or uninterested sellers. Process: find situations where the seller is not price-sensitive (parent shareholders dumping spin-off shares, index deletions), concentrate in 6-8 names. Later the Magic Formula (The Little Book That Beats the Market, 2005): rank by return on capital (EBIT / net working capital + net fixed assets) and earnings yield (EBIT / EV), buy the top 20-30, rebalance yearly; backtest 1988-2004 ~30.8%/yr vs S&P ~12.4% (backtest, not live). Live results of formula funds and many replications were far weaker and long periods of underperformance made most users quit. Mistakes: the public long-short Gotham funds lagged in the 2010s growth era (unverified magnitude). Copyable for an Indian individual: spin-off and demerger watchlist (Indian demergers often sell off as funds exit the new listing), rights-issue and open-offer arbitrage; Magic-Formula-style screen as an idea generator, not a black box.
title: Joel Greenblatt - special situations and the Magic Formula
